title: Repo scaffold
detail: Create the GitHub repo with a src/ and data/ folder, a .gitignore, and requirements.txt. Nothing fancy — just a clean place for everything else to live.

title: NHTSA ingestion script (recalls + complaints)
detail: Write a script that hits NHTSA's recallsByVehicle and complaintsByVehicle endpoints for the target vehicles (Camry, CR-V, F-150) and saves the raw JSON locally.

title: Run ingestion live, verify response shape
detail: Actually run the script against the live API (not just read the code). Open the saved JSON and confirm: is `results` the right key? What fields exist per recall (defect summary, recall number)? Do complaints include readable free-text descriptions? Field names must be confirmed before the embedding step depends on them.

title: Chunk + embed into pgvector
detail: Set up Postgres with the pgvector extension. Chunk recall defect summaries and complaint text into passages, generate embeddings for each, and load them into a vector table.

title: Intent classifier (lookup/search/general)
detail: Build or fine-tune a small classifier that routes a user's question into one of: recall_lookup, complaint_search, or general_question. Reuse an approach you already know from fine-tuning work.

title: RAG retrieval + LLM answer w/ citations
detail: Given a query, retrieve the top-k matching chunks from pgvector and pass them to an LLM to generate an answer that explicitly cites the recall/TSB number it came from — not just a paraphrase.

title: End-to-end script working (question in, answer out)
detail: Wire ingestion → embed → classify → retrieve → generate into a single script or notebook. Correctness over elegance — this is the last purely-ML ticket before infra work starts.

title: Split pipeline into 3 services
detail: Break the single script into three services — intent classifier, retriever, answer generator — each with a clean interface (gRPC or REST) instead of direct function calls.

title: Dockerize each service
detail: Write a Dockerfile per service: multi-stage build, non-root user, and a /healthz endpoint each service exposes for later use by k8s probes.

title: docker-compose local run
detail: Write docker-compose.yml wiring all three services plus pgvector, so `docker-compose up` runs the entire pipeline locally with one command.

title: GitHub Actions CI pipeline
detail: On every push: lint, run tests, build each service's Docker image, and push it to a registry (GHCR is free and simple to start with).

title: Local k8s cluster (kind/minikube)
detail: Install kind or minikube and get a local cluster running. This is where you start applying manifests instead of just docker-compose.

title: Deployments + Services for all 3 apps
detail: Write Deployment + Service manifests for each of the three apps, plus a StatefulSet for pgvector (it needs persistent storage, unlike the stateless services).

title: ConfigMaps / Secrets
detail: Move configuration values into ConfigMaps and anything sensitive (DB credentials, API keys) into Kubernetes Secrets instead of hardcoding them in manifests or images.

title: Readiness / liveness probes
detail: Wire each service's /healthz endpoint into readiness and liveness probes so Kubernetes can detect a hung or crashed pod and restart or stop routing to it.

title: HPA + load test with k6
detail: Add a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on the retriever and answer-generator services. Use k6 or locust to simulate concurrent requests and confirm you can actually watch pods scale up under load.

title: Deploy to real EKS cluster
detail: Provision a real EKS cluster (eksctl is the fastest path to start) and deploy the same manifests from Phase 2 there. Set a billing alert before you do anything else.

title: IAM roles for service accounts
detail: Set up IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) so each pod gets a scoped IAM role instead of long-lived AWS credentials baked into the app.

title: ECR + ALB ingress + VPC basics
detail: Push images to ECR instead of GHCR, expose the app externally via an ALB Ingress Controller, and get familiar with the VPC's public/private subnet split your cluster is using.

title: Terraform: VPC + EKS cluster
detail: Rewrite the EKS cluster and its VPC/networking as Terraform modules instead of the manual eksctl/console setup from Phase 3.

title: terraform apply / destroy workflow
detail: Practice the full plan → apply → destroy cycle end to end. Get comfortable running `terraform destroy` between work sessions — this is your main cost control lever from here on.

title: Prometheus + Grafana setup
detail: Deploy Prometheus to scrape metrics from all three services, connect Grafana to it, and build one basic dashboard as a starting point.

title: Per-stage latency dashboards
detail: Instrument each service to emit its own stage latency (intent classification time, retrieval time, generation time) and chart p50/p95/p99 for each in Grafana, not just an aggregate.

title: OpenTelemetry tracing across services
detail: Add distributed tracing so a single request's full path and per-stage timing is visible end to end — this is what actually answers 'why was this one request slow'.

title: Alerting rules (p95 latency)
detail: Configure an alert (Alertmanager or Grafana alerting) that fires when p95 latency crosses a threshold. Test it for real by artificially slowing down one service and confirming the alert fires.

title: Canary / blue-green rollout for new model
detail: Use Argo Rollouts (or a manual blue-green setup) to ship a new fine-tuned intent classifier version with zero downtime, routing a small percentage of traffic to it first.

title: Secrets via AWS Secrets Manager
detail: Move secrets out of plain Kubernetes Secrets and into AWS Secrets Manager, wired in via something like the external-secrets operator.

title: Cost monitoring / tagging
detail: Tag AWS resources by project, double-check your billing alert is actually working, and dig into where the EKS cluster's cost is really going — idle worker nodes are the usual surprise.

title: Rollback drill (ship bad model, roll back)
detail: Intentionally deploy a deliberately 'bad' model version, notice the regression (via your Phase 5 dashboards), and practice rolling back to the previous version in under a minute.

title: Load test for concurrency ceiling
detail: Run k6/locust at steadily increasing concurrency until the system falls over, and note where the actual ceiling is — this becomes a concrete number for your writeup.

title: Final architecture diagram
detail: Draw the final end-to-end architecture — all services, data flow, and infra — for the README. This is what a reviewer or interviewer will actually look at first.

title: Case-study writeup
detail: Write up what you built, what broke along the way, and what you'd do differently next time. This writeup is what actually gets read in interviews — more than the code itself.
